## Solution

**Claim.** $\mathbb{A}^n(k)$ and $\mathbb{A}^m(k)$ (with the Zariski topology, $k$ algebraically closed) are homeomorphic if and only if $m = n$.

The direction "$m=n \Rightarrow$ homeomorphic" is trivial. We prove the converse.

### Topological invariant: the combinatorial (Krull) dimension

For a topological space $X$, define the **combinatorial dimension**
$$\dim X = \sup\bigl\{\ell : \text{there is a chain } Z_0 \subsetneq Z_1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq Z_\ell \text{ of nonempty irreducible closed subsets of } X\bigr\}.$$

**Irreducibility is a topological property.** A closed subset $Z\subseteq X$ is irreducible iff it is nonempty and cannot be written as $Z = Z_1\cup Z_2$ with $Z_1,Z_2$ proper closed subsets. A homeomorphism $h:X\to Y$ sends closed sets bijectively onto closed sets, preserves inclusion, and preserves finite unions; hence it sends irreducible closed sets to irreducible closed sets and preserves strictness of chains. Therefore

$$X\cong Y \;\Longrightarrow\; \dim X = \dim Y. \tag{$\ast$}$$

### Computing $\dim \mathbb{A}^n(k)$

Since $k$ is algebraically closed, the Nullstellensatz gives an order-reversing bijection
$$\{\text{closed subsets of } \mathbb{A}^n(k)\} \;\longleftrightarrow\; \{\text{radical ideals of } k[x_1,\dots,x_n]\},\qquad V\leftrightarrow I(V).$$
Under this bijection, **irreducible** closed subsets correspond exactly to **prime** ideals (a closed set $V$ is irreducible iff $I(V)$ is prime). Hence chains of nonempty irreducible closed subsets of $\mathbb{A}^n(k)$ of length $\ell$ correspond bijectively to chains of prime ideals of $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ of length $\ell$. Consequently
$$\dim \mathbb{A}^n(k) = \operatorname{Kdim} k[x_1,\dots,x_n].$$

It is a standard theorem (Noether normalization, or the principal ideal theorem inductively) that
$$\operatorname{Kdim} k[x_1,\dots,x_n] = n.$$

*Lower bound:* the chain of prime ideals
$$(0) \subsetneq (x_1) \subsetneq (x_1,x_2) \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq (x_1,\dots,x_n)$$
has length $n$, so $\operatorname{Kdim}\ge n$.

*Upper bound:* by Noether normalization, every prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ has height $\le n$ (equivalently, $\operatorname{trdeg}_k \operatorname{Frac}(k[x_1,\dots,x_n]/\mathfrak p) + \operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p = n$), so no chain of primes can exceed length $n$.

Therefore
$$\dim \mathbb{A}^n(k) = n. \tag{$\dagger$}$$

### Conclusion

Suppose $\mathbb{A}^n(k)\cong \mathbb{A}^m(k)$ as topological spaces. By $(\ast)$ and $(\dagger)$,
$$n = \dim \mathbb{A}^n(k) = \dim \mathbb{A}^m(k) = m.$$

Hence $m=n$. Combined with the trivial converse, the affine spaces $\mathbb{A}^n(k)$ and $\mathbb{A}^m(k)$ are homeomorphic (in the Zariski topology, over an algebraically closed field $k$) **if and only if $m = n$**.

### PROOF COMPLETE
